extracted.intended_audience: recipients under Title IX (college and university administrators, Title IX coordinators, campus legal counsel), policymakers, advocates, and stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory preamble guidance on what schools and other recipients must do when responding to sexual harassment and sexual violence complaints, including required grievance-procedure features, remedial actions, due-process considerations, documentation obligations, and supportive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient obligation to remedy and prevent harassment regardless of notice
rubrics_metrics.description: “The recipient is, therefore, also responsible for remedying any effects of the harassment on the victim, as well as for ending the harassment and preventing its recurrence. This is true whether or not the recipient has `notice' of the harassment.” (2001 Guidance at 10)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must take actions to eliminate harassment, prevent recurrence, and address its effects; effective corrective action may require remedies for the complainant. The obligation to remediate exists even if the institution lacked actual notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: offer and consider complainant's wishes
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.30 (defining “supportive measures”); §106.44(a); §106.45(b)(1). The recipient must offer supportive measures to a complainant, and the Title IX Coordinator must discuss supportive measures with a complainant and consider the complainant's wishes regarding supportive measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures are individualized services. A recipient must offer them promptly as part of its response; if supportive measures are not provided, the recipient must document why that response was not clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances (for example, because the complainant did not want any supportive measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt investigation and resolution even absent formal complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: “Regardless of whether the student who was harassed, or his or her parent, decides to file a formal complaint or otherwise request action on the student's behalf ... the school must promptly investigate to determine what occurred and then take appropriate steps to resolve the situation.” (2001 Guidance at 15)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should promptly investigate observed or reported harassment to determine what occurred and take appropriate steps to resolve the matter, irrespective of whether a formal complaint is filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented justification when not initiating grievance or not providing supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a complainant does not wish to participate, a recipient may sometimes conclude initiating a grievance process is necessary but must have that conclusion reached by the specially trained Title IX Coordinator and must document the reasons why the recipient believes its response was not deliberately indifferent. (§106.44(a); §106.45(b)(10))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recipient decides not to investigate, adjudicate, or provide supportive measures (or otherwise believes its response is sufficient without such steps), it must document its reasons (including complainant wishes) to show the response was not clearly unreasonable given known circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-deliberate indifference standard for recipient responses
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(b)(2) provides that recipient responses to sexual harassment must be non-deliberately indifferent—i.e., not clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances—and must comply with all the specific requirements in §106.44(a), regardless of whether a formal complaint is ever filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of a recipient's response centers on whether actions were clearly unreasonable under the circumstances, and compliance with the specific regulatory requirements (e.g., supportive measures, Title IX Coordinator involvement) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and publish grievance procedures providing prompt and equitable resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are required to have grievance procedures through which students can complain of alleged sex discrimination, including sexual harassment, and to adopt and publish grievance procedures providing for prompt and equitable resolution. (1997 Guidance; 34 CFR 106.8(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures must be publicly available and designed to resolve complaints promptly and equitably; specific mechanics may vary with institution size, audience, and legal context, but the core duties remain. The Department prescribes specific procedural features rather than relying on vague exhortations to provide 'due process.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of an equitable grievance process (investigation, timeframes, notice, opportunity to present evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable grievance procedures must provide for “adequate, reliable, and impartial investigation of complaints, including the opportunity for both parties to present witnesses and other evidence,” “[d]esignated and reasonably prompt time frames for the major stages of the complaint process,” and “[n]otice to the parties of the outcome of the complaint.” (2001 Guidance at 20; 2011 Dear Colleague Letter at 8)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grievance processes should include impartial investigations, timely progression with designated timeframes, notice to parties at key stages and of outcomes, and fair opportunities for both parties to present witnesses and evidence. While formats may differ, these substantive elements are required for 'prompt and equitable' resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal and timely access to information consistent with FERPA and privacy protections
rubrics_metrics.description: “The complainant and the alleged perpetrator must be afforded similar and timely access to any information that will be used at the hearing” consistent with FERPA and while protecting privileged information and withholding from the alleged perpetrator information about the complainant's sexual history. (2011 Dear Colleague Letter at 11, fn.29)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parties should have comparable access to evidence used in the proceeding, subject to FERPA and other privacy/privilege constraints. Institutions must balance transparency and privacy, including withholding irrelevant sexual history evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary sanctions must be proportionate and consider impact of separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanction decisions must be made for the purpose of deciding how best to enforce the school's code of student conduct while considering the impact of separating a student from her or his education. Any disciplinary decision must be made as a proportionate response to the violation. (2001 Guidance at 16; 2017 Q&A at 6)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When imposing disciplinary sanctions (including suspension or expulsion), institutions must calibrate sanctions proportionally and account for educational harm caused by separation; sanctions should serve institutional conduct goals while protecting the rights of involved students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live hearing cross-examination must be conducted by parties' advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post-SB 169 Working Group recommended that cross-examination at a live hearing occur by the parties submitting questions through the decision-maker(s), while the final regulations, §106.45(b)(6)(i), require that the parties' advisors conduct the cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the final regulations, cross-examination at live hearings is performed by each party's advisor rather than by the parties themselves or solely by the decision-maker, although other models were considered by stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies must stop harassment and prevent recurrence; discrete required actions evaluate discretionary decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under prior Department guidance recipients were expected to take actions that 'stop the harassment and prevent its recurrence.' The final regulations instead require a recipient must take specified actions, and a recipient's decisions with respect to discretionary actions are evaluated in light of the known circumstances. (Preamble discussion, paragraph 184)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations enumerate required remedial steps and assess discretionary choices against the facts; simply taking many conceivable measures is not sufficient if the chosen response is unreasonable in light of known circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum due process protections in disciplinary contexts (notice, opportunity to prepare, hearing, impartial decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law and commentary establish the 'bare minimum requirements' of procedural protections: (1) adequate notice of the charges; (2) reasonable opportunity to prepare for and meet them; (3) an orderly hearing adapted to the nature of the case; and (4) a fair and impartial decision. (Goss v. Lopez; Boothe-Perry; Mathews v. Eldridge citations)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether public or private, institutions must ensure these minimum procedural safeguards are provided (public institutions subject to constitutional due process; private institutions subject to fundamental fairness as articulated in their own policies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bias and ensure fairness for both complainant and respondent
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders and commentators note the need to balance victim protection and due process, and that grievance processes have in some instances been biased or flawed. The Department agrees institutions need more training and that the regulations prescribe specific procedural features to protect both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grievance procedures must be designed and implemented to avoid sex-based bias or procedural partiality; training for administrators and clear, specific procedures help ensure balanced protection of complainants' and respondents' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations do not import criminal-law protections or standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not permit application of the criminal standard of evidence (beyond a reasonable doubt), do not grant respondents a right of self-representation with respect to confronting witnesses, do not grant respondents a right to effective assistance of counsel, and do not purport to protect respondents from 'double jeopardy' (i.e., by preventing a complainant from appealing a determination of non-responsibility). (Preamble paragraph 225)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title IX grievance processes are civil/administrative in nature; institutions should not treat them as criminal proceedings and need not (and should not be required to) grant criminal-law-specific procedural protections beyond those the regulations prescribe.
